analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and agencies to tell people when hackers get their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after introduction in June 2006 it was referred to three House committees and then to a subcommittee, where it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal agencies and businesses in interstate commerce to notify people whose Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, or financial account numbers were taken in a data breach. It set deadlines for notice, required a toll-free number and credit bureau contact information in each notice, let the FTC and state attorneys general impose fines of up to $1,000 per affected person or $50,000 per day for failures to notify, and made it easier for breach victims to place fraud alerts on their credit files. It would also have overridden state laws inconsistent with its specific requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal data is held by companies and agencies. Today most states have their own breach-notification laws, but in 2006 there was no federal requirement, and people often learned their Social Security number had been stolen only after fraud appeared on their credit. The bill would have guaranteed notice after any breach, a description of what was taken, a phone number to call, and credit bureau contacts so victims could act quickly. It also let breach victims place fraud alerts on their credit files.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose personal data is breached

how_it_helps.text: Required any federal agency or business that owns, licenses, or collects personal information to notify individuals whose Social Security number, driver's license number, or account or card number was, or was reasonably believed to have been, taken by an unauthorized person [S2] [S3].

Required notice without unreasonable delay, put the burden on the company to prove its notifications and any delays were proper, and required each notice to describe what information was taken, include a toll-free number, and list the major credit reporting agencies' contact information [S3].

Set fines of up to $1,000 per affected individual or $50,000 per day for failure to notify, enforceable by the FTC, and let state attorneys general sue on behalf of their residents to get injunctions, damages, and restitution [S3].

Amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that receiving a breach notice would itself qualify a consumer to place a fraud alert on their credit file, making it easier for breach victims to block new accounts opened in their name [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and federal agencies that hold personal data, which would bear the cost of monitoring for breaches, notifying affected individuals, and paying fines for failures to notify. A large company with a breach affecting more than 500,000 people could avoid mailing individual notices and instead post notice on its website and alert major media, keeping notification costs down.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies and agencies holding personal data

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede inconsistent state laws on the conduct it requires, which could replace stronger or broader state breach-notification protections with the federal floor in this bill [S3].

Companies could use cheaper website and media notices instead of direct notice when a breach affects more than 500,000 people or direct notice would cost over $500,000, meaning the people affected by the largest breaches would get the least direct warning [S3].

The remedies are fines and injunctions enforceable by regulators and state attorneys general; the bill does not create a private right to sue, and the $50,000-per-day cap may be small relative to the harm from a breach exposing millions of records [S3].

Federal agencies could delay or skip notification for national security or law-enforcement reasons by written certification, subject only to limits on using certifications to conceal wrongdoing and a requirement to notify Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: guaranteed, prompt notice after a breach, plus easier fraud alerts, helps people freeze identity theft before it does lasting damage. The main honest objections are that the bill would preempt some state protections, and that its substitute-notice option lets the companies holding the data notify the largest breaches most cheaply. Even so, in 2006 a federal notice requirement with enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general would have been a meaningful improvement for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, then to a subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Lantos introduced the Notification of Risk to Personal Data Act on June 12, 2006 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Government Reform, and Financial Services, with the Speaker to determine how it would be divided among them [S5].
On June 23, 2006, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, and no further action was taken [S5].
No cosponsors signed on to the bill [S4].
The bill never received a committee markup, floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and federal agencies holding Americans' personal data were better off, because they continued to face no federal requirement to tell people when their Social Security numbers or account information were stolen. Consumers gained nothing from this bill's failure; the many state breach-notification laws that later filled the gap did not exist in most states at the time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies holding personal data, untouched by federal rules

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever taken, so the record shows only a Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Companies and agencies holding consumer personal data (retailers, financial firms, data brokers)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed notification duties and fines on anyone holding personal data, but its preemption clause would have replaced a patchwork of state rules with one federal standard, and its substitute-notice option let them handle the largest breaches cheaply. Its failure left them facing no federal notification duty at all in 2006.

The bill required breach notifiers to coordinate with the nationwide credit bureaus when notifying over 1,000 people and to include bureau contact information in every notice, routing breach responses through them. The expanded fraud-alert provision also sent more consumers to the bureaus to place alerts.
